title: Ed Tech Can Be Good, Too
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman examines a mini-study of Khan Academy used as a supplemental math tool in 13 Newark, New Jersey schools over three years (approximately 6,700 students, 87% qualifying for free/reduced lunch). The results are notable on several fronts: 70% of students met the recommended usage threshold of 30 minutes daily -- far above the typical 'five percent problem' -- average math gains were small but positive, gains scaled linearly with engagement, and most strikingly, the largest gains accrued to the lowest-performing students. Aldeman argues this finding directly addresses post-pandemic achievement recovery, since low-performing students have been hardest hit. The key insight is not that Khan Academy is uniquely powerful, but that when engagement is high, even widely-criticized tools deliver measurable outcomes.
points: * The 'five percent problem' -- the observation that most students don't engage with ed tech apps enough to see benefits -- was largely avoided: 70% of Newark students met recommended usage thresholds. * Returns were linear: students who used Khan Academy more and completed more lessons learned more -- confirming engagement as the fundamental variable in ed tech effectiveness. * Most important finding: the largest math gains by far were for level 1 (lowest-performing) students, directly addressing the group most severely affected by pandemic learning loss. * The study challenges reflexive ed tech dismissal by showing that the critical variable is implementation quality and actual use, not the technology's intrinsic power. * 87% of the 6,700 students qualified for free or reduced-price lunch -- making the engagement rates and outcomes especially notable for high-need populations. * Aldeman concludes: 'Schools and districts have tools available to address one of their biggest challenges. But students have to actually use those tools to see any benefits.'
quotes: There's plenty of research suggesting that high-quality apps like Khan Academy are helpful, but only for the kids who actually use them regularly.
Engagement really is the holy grail of learning.
When the authors sorted the effects of Khan Academy implementation across performance levels the largest effects, by far, were for the lowest-performing students.
Schools and districts have tools available to address one of their biggest challenges. But students have to actually use those tools to see any benefits.
